title: Media Ownership
blurb: Concentration, regulation and the platforms — parliament on the press.

brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about media ownership?
brief.answer:
The parliamentary record shows that Australia’s commercial media were already extraordinarily concentrated before the 2002 ownership changes were attempted, and that this concentration was the central fact driving the debate. Labor MPs repeatedly cited figures showing News Ltd controlled roughly two-thirds of capital city and national newspaper circulation, three-quarters of Sunday newspapers, about half of suburban newspapers and a quarter of regional newspapers, with a quarter stake in pay TV operator Foxtel. PBL was said to control three metropolitan and one regional television licence reaching more than half the potential audience, a quarter of Foxtel, a third of Sky News, sixty-five magazines and about forty per cent of the top-thirty magazine circulation. A later speaker put News Ltd’s share at 49 per cent of regional newspapers, 67 per cent of national and metropolitan dailies and 76 per cent of Sunday papers, while the International Federation of Journalists was quoted saying News Corp controlled nearly 70 per cent of metropolitan newspapers by circulation. Opposition speakers argued that further concentration would reduce Australia’s roughly six major commercial media players to as few as three, and that this threatened democracy because most Australians still got news from television, radio and newspapers rather than from the internet or pay TV.

The debate shifted over time from a government proposal to abolish cross-media and foreign ownership rules almost entirely, to a narrower but still controversial plan. The original 2002 bill, introduced by Senator Alston, proposed removing all existing cross-media and foreign ownership restrictions and replacing them with Australian Broadcasting Authority “editorial separation” certificates allowing mergers if newsrooms were supposedly kept independent. After opposition inside the Coalition and in the Senate, the government amended the bill to allow ownership of only two of the three media types in regional markets, and later in all markets. Labor and crossbench speakers treated this as a tacit admission that cross-media regulation was still needed. The Senate then passed the bill with an amendment by Senator Harradine, supported by Labor and minor party senators, that specifically prohibited one proprietor owning both a newspaper and a television station in the same market. The government rejected that amendment, the bill was laid aside, and the same legislation was reintroduced as Bill [No. 2]—which speakers said was designed to create a double dissolution trigger.

The sharpest disagreement was over whether ownership determines media content and influence. Government supporters argued that ownership “per se is irrelevant,” that new technologies provided a plethora of sources, and that editorial separation certificates plus general competition and foreign investment laws were enough to protect diversity. Opponents—including Labor, the Australian Press Council, the Communications Law Centre, the journalists’ union and small regional broadcasters—said this was a “fig leaf” and that “he who pays the piper calls the tune.” They warned that the ABA certificate system would be ineffective in guaranteeing diversity but would create a dangerous mechanism for future governments to interfere with or intimidate media organisations. The Australian Press Council was quoted as telling the minister that the editorial separation regime was a severe threat to press freedom. Speakers also pointed to the government’s own earlier backbench warnings against media concentration from ministers who later stayed silent, calling this hypocrisy.

What was promised was greater diversity, competition and access to capital through modernised ownership rules and increased foreign investment. What was reported to have happened was the opposite: the bill was widely described as serving the interests of Rupert Murdoch and Kerry Packer, the two dominant proprietors, by letting them buy newspapers, television and radio in the same market. When the Senate delivered a bill that kept the newspaper-television ban but still removed radio from cross-media limits and eliminated foreign ownership restrictions, the government abandoned it. Opponents said this revealed the real agenda: because the amended bill stopped PBL buying Fairfax and News Ltd buying a television network, the major proprietors preferred no change at all, and the government rejected three-quarters of its own reform package rather than lose that core prize.

sections.question: What have MPs said about media ownership concentration in Australia?
sections.answer:
Based on the provided context, many MPs spoke about media ownership concentration in Australia. Opposition MPs, particularly from the Labor Party, argued that further concentration of media ownership is a grave threat to democracy, reduces diversity of opinion, and serves the interests of media proprietors rather than the public. They said Australia already has one of the most concentrated media industries in the world, and that the Broadcasting Services Amendment (Media Ownership) Bill 2002 would make this worse by allowing one proprietor to own newspapers, television stations, and radio stations in the same market.

Several MPs quoted past statements from government members who had previously warned against media concentration, accusing them of hypocrisy for now supporting the bill. They also said concentrated ownership could lead to fewer journalists, less independent reporting, and greater influence by media moguls over politics and public opinion.

Some government-supporting MPs spoke in favour of the bill, arguing that existing laws were outdated, that media needed to compete globally, and that safeguards like editorial separation and minimum media group tests would protect diversity. One ministerial answer acknowledged that the bill does allow further concentration of media ownership, but said this was justified by the government's election commitment to reform media ownership laws.
